- `scatter`: number (default 0.6) — How far from home, and how turned, the tipped-out pieces lie, 0 (just above their slots) to 1 (anywhere in the tray, up to 28°).
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — Play a snap as a piece placed by hand is pulled in and a click as it locks. The automatic assembly is silent.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — The puzzle still assembles itself; pieces cannot be moved.
- `className`: string — Sizes the tray; the default is aspect-[4/3] w-full.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the loose pieces are one roving group — Left and Right move through them in reading order, Up and Down by row, Home and End jump — and Enter or Space places the focused piece, the same end state as dragging it home, with focus moving on to the next loose piece and to the picture after the last.
- Reduced motion: nothing travels or bounces — pieces fade in where they lie, each placement is an instant move into its slot, and the last piece waits there at half strength until ready; dragging still follows the pointer directly.
- The tray's rim is exactly the tabs' reach, so pieces lying about and their focus rings stay inside the box; the cut is clipped with objectBoundingBox clip paths, so it renders the same on the server and at any size.

### Etch Reveal (KQ-1210) — `etch-reveal`
Drawn with two knobs.

An image placeholder that is a drawing toy: while the picture loads, one continuous line traced from its own contours runs across a powder screen at a steady mechanical pace, the left knob turning with the stylus's x and the right with its y, and when the line is done and the picture is ready the powder fades into the picture on the enter ease. Turning either knob — dragged round its centre, or by arrow keys, since both are real sliders — draws by hand while the tracing waits, and a turned knob settles on springs.snap. Dragging the frame side to side shakes the toy, rubber-banded within its own padding and settling on springs.snap with the release velocity, and every stroke knocks powder back over the line until the screen is clear; the Shake plate does the same from the keyboard.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/etch-reveal`

Props:
- `alt`: string — What the picture shows. Always its accessible name: the picture's role="img" label, or the img's own alt for src.
- `src`: string — The picture's address. Without it, children is the picture.
- `children`: ReactNode — The finished picture when there is no src: an inline SVG or an image, sized to fill the box.
- `ready`: boolean — Controlled: the picture may show. Uncontrolled, it is ready once the picture exists (a src has loaded or failed) and the line has been drawn.
- `progress`: number — 0 to 1, while not ready: how far the effect may come, for a determinate load.
- `onReady`: () => void — Fires once per load, when the effect has resolved and the picture is whole.
- `speed`: number (default 1) — How fast the stylus draws by itself, 0.5 to 2.
- `frame`: "red" | "teal" | "ink" (default "red") — The toy's colour, a fixed pigment in either theme.
- `line`: number (default 2) — The stylus's line, 1 to 3 px.
- `ratio`: number (default 2) — The screen's width over its height.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — Play the stylus scraping while the visitor turns a knob, and the powder rushing while they shake. Every loop stops on release, key up or blur; the automatic drawing is silent.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — The toy still draws and resolves; knobs and shaking are off.
- `className`: string — Sizes the toy; the default is w-full.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the knobs are sliders named Across and Up and down — arrow keys turn them a step (Shift for five), Page keys ten percent, Home and End run to the stops, and a held key draws a continuous line; the Shake plate is a button that shakes the screen clear, the same end state as dragging the frame side to side.
- Reduced motion: the traced line appears in six still steps with no running stylus, the knobs jump to their angles and the frame never moves; each reversal of a drag still fades the drawing, the Shake plate fades it at once, and the picture resolves with a short fade.
- The line is traced from the picture's own pixels (an inline SVG is read with its computed colours); before the picture shows, shaking clears the traced line too and the toy traces it again, and after it shows, shaking clears only what the visitor drew over it.

### Sun Arc (KQ-1211) — `sun-arc`
Where the day has got to.

A daylight widget: the sun rides a sine arch from first to last light over a horizon whose sky, ground, glow and stars take the hour's colours, with the daylight left read beside it. Press anywhere in the sky and the sun comes to the finger on the flick spring, follows it 1:1 along the arch and rubber-bands past dawn and dusk; a release projects the throw and the sun glides to the landing on the glide spring with the release velocity, ticking once per hour crossed. The rail under the panel lines up with the arch and is a real slider: arrow keys step the time, Page keys an hour, Home and End jump to first and last light, and Escape or the Now pill brings the sun back to the present.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/sun-arc`

Props:
- `sunrise`: number — Sunrise, in minutes after local midnight (06:14 is 374).
- `sunset`: number — Sunset, in minutes after local midnight.
- `dawn`: number (default sunrise - 30) — First light, in minutes after midnight: where the arc's left tail ends.
- `dusk`: number (default sunset + 30) — Last light, in minutes after midnight: where the arc's right tail ends.
- `now`: Date | number — The live moment the sun follows while the value is null. Pass it, with timeZone, to render on the server; without it the widget keeps its own clock after hydration.
- `timeZone`: string — The IANA time zone now is read in, e.g. "UTC". Defaults to the runtime's own.
- `value / defaultValue`: number | null (default null) — The time shown, in minutes after midnight; null follows now.
- `onValueChange`: (value: number | null) => void — Fires from the drag, tap, key or Now press that changed the time shown (null when it returns to now).
- `step`: number (default 5) — Minutes per arrow key, and the grid a scrub lands on.
- `clock`: "12" | "24" (default "24") — Print every time in 24-hour (06:14) or 12-hour (6:14 am) form.
- `sky`: boolean (default true) — Paint the sky, ground, horizon glow and stars with the hour. Off leaves a quiet panel on the card surface.
- `marks`: boolean (default true) — Show the dawn and dusk marks with their times, and a dot on the arc for every whole hour.
- `label`: string (default "Daylight") — The widget's name: the group's and the slider's accessible name, shown over the reading when there is room.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — Tick once per whole hour the visitor scrubs past, pitched by the sun's height, and brighter at sunrise and sunset.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — Shows the day but takes no drag or keys.
- `className`: string — Classes for the widget's root.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the rail is a slider from first to last light — Left/Right (and Down/Up) step `step` minutes, Page Up/Down an hour, Home and End jump to dawn and dusk, and Escape returns to now (handled only when scrubbed). The sky's drag mirrors it for pointers, and the Now pill is a real button.
- Reduced motion: the sun never glides — a throw lands where it was let go and keys jump — while the sky, the reading and the stars still change with the time, because they are the information. The drag itself stays 1:1.
- Pass now and timeZone for server rendering; sunrise, sunset, dawn and dusk are wall-clock minutes in that zone. While live, sunrise, sunset and last light are announced once each as the clock reaches them.

### Moon Phase (KQ-1212) — `moon-phase`
Tonight's moon, and the next.

A moon widget whose lit part is computed from the date — the elongation with its six largest periodic terms — and drawn as the bright limb closed by the terminator's half ellipse, with the phase's name, the share lit and the next full and new moon beside it. A drag across the moon moves through the nights with the terminator travelling under the finger (its own width is a week), and a release projects the throw and glides to the nearest whole night on the glide spring with the release velocity, ticking once per night; the Full and New rows glide the moon to their nights, and seen from the south the whole moon turns over on glide. The night tile is a slider: arrow keys step a night, Page keys a week, Home and End the reach, and Escape or the Tonight pill returns to tonight.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/moon-phase`

Props:
- `now`: Date | number — Tonight: the moment the scrub counts from. Pass it, with timeZone, to render on the server; without it the widget keeps its own clock after hydration.
- `timeZone`: string — The IANA time zone the dates are written in, e.g. "UTC". Defaults to the runtime's own.
- `value / defaultValue`: number (default 0) — The night shown, in whole days from now (0 is tonight).
- `onValueChange`: (value: number) => void — Fires from the drag, key or button that changed the night shown.
- `range`: number (default 60) — How far the scrub reaches each way, in days.
- `hemisphere`: "north" | "south" (default "north") — Which way up the moon is seen: south turns it over (the light on the other side, the seas upside down) and flips the drag so the shadow still follows the finger.
- `detail`: boolean (default true) — Draw the near side's seas, a few craters with rays and the limb's shading. Off: a flat, graphic moon.
- `glow`: number (default 0.5) — The halo's size and strength, 0 to 1; it also follows how much of the moon is lit.
- `label`: string (default "Moon") — The widget's accessible name; the slider is named after it.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — Tick once per night the visitor scrubs past, pitched by how much is lit, and distinctly at full and new.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — Shows the night but takes no drag, keys or buttons.
- `className`: string — Classes for the widget's root.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the night tile is a slider — Left/Right (and Down/Up) step a night, Page Up/Down a week, Home and End go to the ends of range, and Escape returns to tonight (handled only when away). The Full moon, New moon and Tonight controls are buttons with full names.
- Reduced motion: nothing glides or turns over — a key, a throw, a row or the hemisphere swaps straight to its night or view — while the drag still moves the terminator under the finger and the share lit, the name and the dates still update.
- The module also exports moonOn(date), which returns the phase's name, the share lit and whether the moon is waxing, for text elsewhere in a product.

### Egg Timer (KQ-1213) — `egg-timer`
Twist to set, and it rings.

A mechanical kitchen timer, face on: drag round the dial and it turns 1:1 with the hand and ratchets, lingering on each minute's detent and clicking across to the next, rubber-bands past zero and the top of the scale, and lands on the nearest detent on the snap spring when let go, which starts it. While it runs the dial turns back to zero, stepping once a second on the flick spring as the escapement lever rocks on snap (or sweeping silently with ticking off), a red band shrinks toward the pointer, and at zero the shell rattles about its feet on a keyframed tween while the bell rings; a tap pauses and resumes. The dial is a slider in minutes: arrows add or take a minute, Page keys five, Home clears and End sets the whole scale, a held key holds the count like a hand on the dial, and Space or Enter pauses.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/egg-timer`

Props:
- `value / defaultValue`: number (default 0) — Seconds left.
- `onValueChange`: (value: number) => void — Fires with the seconds left: on each detent while setting, on each key step, and once a second while running (while on screen; it catches up on return).
- `running / defaultRunning`: boolean (default false) — Whether it is counting down.
- `onRunningChange`: (running: boolean) => void — Fires from the release, key, tap or ring that started or stopped it.
- `onRing`: () => void — Fires when the count reaches zero and the bell rings.
- `max`: number (default 60) — The scale in minutes, 15 to 60: the graduations, the numbers (every 5, or every 10 past 30) and the size of each ratchet step.
- `shell`: "pear" | "lemon" | "mint" (default "lemon") — The shell's colour, at a fixed lightness so it reads the same in either theme.
- `ticking`: boolean (default true) — Step once a second with the escapement rocking (and a quiet tick-tock, with sound); off, the dial sweeps back smoothly and silently.
- `label`: string (default "Timer") — What is being timed: shown over the reading and used in the dial's name ("Eggs timer").
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — Detents while setting, a tick a second while running and the bell's chime — only once someone has set it (a visitor's turn, key, tap or button, or a host change after mount).
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — Keeps counting, but takes no drag, keys or button.
- `className`: string — Classes for the timer's root.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the dial is a slider in whole minutes — Up/Right add a minute (to the next whole minute), Down/Left take one, Page Up/Down five, Home clears and End sets the whole scale; a held key holds the count and letting go starts it, as letting go of the dial does. Space or Enter pauses and resumes, and the Pause/Start button does the same.
- Reduced motion: nothing springs, rocks or rattles — the dial jumps to each detent and each second, and the ring is the marks flaring — while the drag still turns the dial under the hand, the band and the reading still count down, and the chime still plays.
- The count runs from a deadline, so it keeps real time behind a hidden page or off screen; its once-a-second steps and reports rest there and catch up on return, and the bell is its own timeout so onRing fires on time.

### Plant Care (KQ-1214) — `plant-care`
It droops when it's thirsty.

A plant-care widget whose plant shows how thirsty it is: as the days since watering pass, a fern's fronds flatten until their tips hang over the rim, a monstera's stalks bend and its split leaves hang, a cactus thins and lets its arms sag, the green drains toward straw and the soil dries and cracks, all rebuilt each frame from analytic curves. Pressing Water brings a can in over the pot and tips it on the snap spring, a seeded shower falls in real arcs and splashes while a wet patch spreads, and when the last drops land the leaves spring back up centre first on a staggered snap; a pointer brushed through the plant flicks the leaves it crosses, crisply when watered and loosely when thirsty. The Water button is the whole keyboard path, and the next watering day is named from `now`.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/plant-care`

Props:
- `days / defaultDays`: number (default 5) — Days since the plant was last watered: its thirst, and so its pose, its colour and the soil.
- `onDaysChange`: (days: number) => void — Fires from the Water press with 0.
- `plant`: "fern" | "monstera" | "cactus" (default "fern") — Which plant is drawn: arching fronds, split leaves on stalks, or a column with two arms that flowers when well watered. It also sets the default interval.
- `pot`: "clay" | "stone" | "glaze" (default "clay") — The pot's finish: terracotta, speckled stone, or a deep blue glaze over a bare clay foot.
- `name`: string (default "Fern", "Monstera" or "Cactus") — The plant's name: the widget's title and its accessible name.
- `interval`: number (default 4 / 7 / 10 by plant) — Days between waterings. Thirst is days over interval: droop starts at a third of it and is complete at 1.4 times it.
- `now`: number | Date — The current moment. With it the next watering day is named ("Next Sun 11 Oct"); without it, counted ("Next in 3 days").
- `utcOffset`: number (default 0) — Minutes east of UTC used to read `now` as a calendar day, so server and client agree.
- `waterLabel`: string (default "Water") — The button's text.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — After a Water press: the pour loop while water leaves the can, and a plip as the first, middle and last drops land, rising as the soil fills. Brushing and host changes are silent.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — The button is disabled, brushing does nothing, and a watering in progress finishes at once.
- `className`: string — Classes for the root, a container up to max-w-xs.

Notes:
- Keyboard: Water is a real button — Enter or Space waters the plant through the same choreography as a press, and it is aria-disabled (focus stays) until the watering ends. Brushing the leaves is decoration and changes no state. A polite live region says "Sill fern watered. Next watering Sunday 11 October." or, when the host changes the days, how long since watering and when it is due.
- Reduced motion: no can travel, flying drops, sway or springs — the can fades in already tipped over a still shower, the soil darkens, the can fades out and the leaves swap to their new pose while the green returns; the pour and plips still answer the press.
- Controlled: onDaysChange(0) fires from the press; the leaves perk up to whatever days the host holds when the water lands, so a host that refuses the watering keeps its plant thirsty. Pass `now` (and `utcOffset`) for a named next day that renders the same on the server.

### Bin Day (KQ-1215) — `bin-day`
Which one goes out tonight.

A collection-day widget: two to four wheelie bins stand in a row by the house and the one due this collection has been rolled to the kerb, with its name, when it goes out and the bin after it in the header. - `onDayChange`: (day: BinDayWeekday) => void — Fires from the week strip with the chosen weekday.
- `done / defaultDone`: boolean (default false) — This collection's bin has been dealt with: it stands back in the row. Uncontrolled, it is kept for that collection's date only, so the next bin rolls out once the date passes.

- `bins`: number (default 3) — How many bins take turns, one per collection, 2 to 4: Rubbish, Recycling, Garden, Food.
- `colours`: "council" | "pastel" | "mono" (default "council") — Strong civic pigments, soft pastels, or greys told apart by the signs on their fronts. Fixed pigments, the same in either theme.
- `names`: string[] — Names for the bins, in rotation order.
- `offset`: number (default 0) — Shifts which bin a week starts the rotation on (weeks start on Monday).
- `utcOffset`: number (default 0) — Minutes east of UTC used to read `now` as a calendar day.
- `label`: string (default "Bin day") — The widget's accessible name.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — A thud when a bin the visitor sent lands at the kerb, a tick when it arrives back in the row, a lighter tick per day stepped on the strip. Host changes are silent.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — Done, the strip and the drag do nothing.
- `className`: string — Classes for the root, a container up to max-w-xs.

Notes:
- Keyboard: Done and Undo are a real button ("Mark Recycling done", "Undo: Recycling back out") and reach the same end states as dragging the bin; the week strip is a radiogroup with roving focus, where arrows move and choose, and Home and End jump to the first and last day. A polite live region speaks a sentence frozen at each change, such as "Recycling done. Next: Garden, Thursday 15 October."
- Reduced motion: nothing tips, rolls, rocks or opens — a bin swaps between its row slot and the kerb at once and the pill swaps days, while the header, chip and tags still change; a drag still follows the finger and lands at once.
- The scene is a role="img" with a sentence of where every bin stands. Only the due bin is draggable (touch-pan-x, so a vertical drag on it never scrolls the page); a tap on it rattles its lid.

### Commute Line (KQ-1216) — `commute-line`
Where the train is now.

A transit widget: the line's pill and direction, a delay badge whose figure rolls on the snap spring, a line diagram of stops with the train on it, and the chosen stop's arrival time. The train's position comes from the timetable, `now` and the delay (or a live `position`), with a dwell at each stop and a cosine pull-away and braking between them; each report moves the shown train there — at the pace steady reports set, so it reads as one continuous glide, or on the drift spring with its own velocity for a first or irregular report — and a jump back to the start is a fade, never a reverse. A window of stops follows the train and the chosen stop on glide and can be dragged sideways; each stop the train reaches pulses; the stops are a radio group where a tap or the arrow keys choose one and an ETA flag hops there on snap.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/commute-line`

- `now`: number | Date — The current moment. Each new value is a report: the train moves to where the timetable and delay put it.
- `delay`: number (default 0) — How late the train is running, in minutes: the badge (on time, late, very late from 6), every ETA, and where the train is.
- `position`: number — A reported position from a live feed, as a fractional stop index (2.4 is 40% of the way from the third stop to the fourth). Overrides the timetable's.
- `stops`: number (default 6) — How many stops the diagram shows at once, 2 to 8. Labels drop to two rows when the spacing is too small for one.
- `line`: "red" | "green" | "blue" (default "blue") — The line's colour, a fixed pigment that reads in either theme, and its default name.
- `label`: string (default "Blue line") — The line's name: its pill and the widget's accessible name.
- `direction`: string — Where the train is heading, shown beside the pill, e.g. "to Harbour".
- `value / defaultValue`: string (default the next stop ahead of the train) — The chosen stop's id: its ETA flag and the footer.
- `onValueChange`: (id: string) => void — Fires from a tap or a key that chose a stop.
- `utcOffset`: number (default 0) — Minutes east of UTC for the clock times shown, so the server and the page agree.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — A chime when the visitor chooses a stop, higher the sooner the train gets there and low for a stop it has left. Reports and arrivals are silent.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — The train still moves; stops cannot be chosen and the line cannot be dragged.
- `className`: string — Classes for the root, a container up to max-w-[40rem].

Notes:
- Keyboard: the stops are a radiogroup with roving focus — arrows choose the next or previous stop, Home and End the first and last, and the window slides to keep the choice in view, which is also the keyboard path for dragging the line. Each radio is named with its ETA ("Fieldline, in 10 minutes, 08:57"). A polite live region speaks a sentence frozen at each change that matters: a choice, a delay change, the train arriving at the chosen stop.
- Reduced motion: the train, the window and the flag jump to each report, the arrival pulse is a flash without growth, and the badge swaps; every time, fill and position still updates.
- The host owns the clock: pass a fixed `now` for the first render and advance it in an effect (and pause that while off screen), so the server and the page render the same train.

### Wind Sock (KQ-1219) — `wind-sock`
Which way, and how hard.

A wind widget: an airfield windsock on a mast in the middle of a compass rose painted on the grass, built from six hoops projected from 3D so it points the way the wind blows in depth as well as across, with its shadow falling downwind on the rose. It hangs at calm and fills toward level by fifteen knots on the glide spring, its five stripes light one by one with the Beaufort bands and turn red from a near gale, and while it is on screen it flaps with a ripple and a seeded wander that grow with gust. Dragging on the rose moves the wind marker 1:1 and the sock swings after it on a hunting vane spring; arrow keys turn the preview 5°, Page keys 45°, Home faces north, and Escape or Live returns to the real wind.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/wind-sock`

Props:
- `speed`: number — Wind speed in knots: how full the sock is, which stripes are lit, how fast it flaps and the reading.
- `direction`: number — The bearing the wind blows from, in degrees (270 is a westerly). The sock points the other way.
- `gust`: number (default 0.35) — How gusty it is, 0 to 1: how hard the sock wanders and swells, and the reading's steady, gusty or very gusty.
- `value / defaultValue`: number | null (default null) — The previewed bearing the sock is shown in, or null for the live wind.
- `onValueChange`: (bearing: number | null) => void — Fires from the drag, tap, key or Live press that changed the preview.
- `label`: string (default "Wind") — The widget's name, used in the slider's name and the band announcements.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — A whoosh as the visitor swings the sock (on a drag at most every 45° and 220 ms, a tap, a key, and the return to live), pitched up with the wind. The flapping itself is silent.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — Keeps showing the wind, but takes no drag, tap or keys.
- `className`: string — Classes for the tile.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the picture is a slider in degrees — Right/Up turn the preview 5° clockwise, Left/Down 5° anticlockwise, Page Up/Down 45°, Home faces north; Escape returns to the live wind and is handled (with preventDefault) only while previewing. The Live button does the same.
- Reduced motion: nothing flaps or hunts — the sock is drawn still and turns and fills on short tweens — while the stripes, the reading and the preview marker still change.
- The flap loop runs only while the sock is on screen, the page is visible and the wind is above calm; a change of Beaufort band is announced once in a polite live region.

### Parking Meter (KQ-1220) — `parking-meter`
Time left on the meter.

A parking meter widget: in the classic style a needle sweeps down a cream dial through the time left, in the digital style seven-segment digits and a ten-bar graph show it, and both read one motion value. Tapping the meter or its button drops a coin into the slot on an accelerating tween as it turns edge-on, it clacks as it lands, and the needle kicks up to the new time on the recoil spring, overshooting against its stop pin and ticking past each mark; a full meter bounces the coin back out. In the last minutes the window's rim pulses and the red flag peeks over the sill, popping up on recoil at expiry; the add button is the keyboard's way in, and the time left is announced at the thresholds and after every coin.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/parking-meter`

Props:
- `now`: Date | number — The moment it is. Pass it, with timeZone, to render on the server; without it the meter keeps its own clock after hydration.
- `timeZone`: string — The IANA time zone times are shown in, e.g. "UTC". Defaults to the runtime's own.
- `value / defaultValue`: number | null (default null) — The moment the meter is paid until, in ms. Null or past is expired.
- `onValueChange`: (paidUntil: number) => void — Fires as each coin lands, with the new paid-until moment.
- `max`: number (default 120) — The longest stay, in minutes: the dial's scale and marks, and the cap a coin cannot pass.
- `coin`: number (default 20) — Minutes one coin buys: the slot plate, the button and how far the needle kicks.
- `style`: "classic" | "digital" (default "classic") — An enamel dome with a needle dial, or a charcoal digital head with an LCD of segment digits and bars.
- `warnAt`: number (default 10) — Minutes left at which the window starts to pulse, the flag to peek and the reading turns the warning colour.
- `label`: string (default "Parking") — What is parked, shown over the reading and used in its announcements.
- `onRefuse`: () => void — A coin refused because the meter is already at max.
- `sound`: boolean (default false) — The coin's clack (a low one when refused) and a tick for each mark the needle passes on its kick, only after a visitor's tap or press. Time passing is silent.
- `disabled`: boolean (default false) — Keeps counting down, but takes no coins.
- `className`: string — Classes for the tile.

Notes:
- Keyboard: the Add button is a real button — Enter or Space drops one coin, exactly as a tap on the meter drawing does (the drawing is a pointer convenience and hidden from assistive technology). The time left is a meter (aria-valuetext "23 minutes left").
- Reduced motion: the coin fades in at the slot instead of falling, the needle and digits move on a short tween with no kick, the flag fades in rather than rising and the rim is a steady amber or red; the reading, the flag and the announcements are unchanged.
- A polite live region speaks warnAt minutes left, one minute left and expiry once each as time passes, and every coin ("Added 20 minutes. 32 minutes left, paid until 14:52.") or refusal.

- Length is delegated to stage-progress; the rail is the promise that this ends.
- Focus follows the frame after the first move, never on first paint — landing on the page must not yank the viewport.
- Questions slide from the direction of travel, so Back reads as going back.

### Open Bench Team (KB-272) — `team-open-bench`
The seats you have not filled are also the team.

### Case Column Testimonial (KB-273) — `testimonial-case-column`

One customer, told at length: a single narrow column of narrative with the measured results pinned in the margin and one line lifted out onto the balance instrument. ### Margin Notes Content (KB-274) — `content-margin-notes`
Argument, not assertion.

An editorial passage with its annotations in the margin, aligned to the paragraph each one belongs to — the shape of a marked-up document rather than a marketing page. ### Live Floor Social Proof (KB-275) — `proof-live-floor`
Somewhere it is 06:40.

Proof as the floor itself, running: a live feed of what is happening across every yard right now, arriving on the conveyor with the standing counts above it. Where the evidence band assembles a case from logos, metrics, and a quote, this one makes the simpler and harder argument — that the thing is in use at this moment, and here is it happening.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/proof-live-floor`

- `counts`: FloorCount[] — The standing numbers above the feed.

Notes:
- Rotation is deterministic — the server renders tick 0 and the client walks the same pool, so there is no hydration drift and no clock.
- Each arrival gets a fresh row key; reusing an event id would read to the conveyor as a reorder, not an arrival.
- Never name customers in the feed. Coarse places are proof; a customer list is a leak.
- Ages come from row position, not timestamps — nothing here needs to be true to the second to be honest.

### Credit Packs Pricing (KB-284) — `pricing-credit-packs`
The discount is checkable, not asserted.

### Ring Set Stats (KB-289) — `stats-ring-set`
Comparable at a glance, defined in plain words.

Notes:

- Let the weakest number in; four numbers above ninety persuade nobody.

### Incident Log Trust (KB-290) — `trust-incident-log`

### Branching Intake Step Form (KB-302) — `stepform-branching-intake`

- The owner line is the reason to choose this over a wizard: name who else is needed.
- Minutes must be honest. A section marked 3 min that takes twenty is worse than no estimate.

### Founders Note Team (KB-304) — `team-founders-note`
Answerable for, not titled as.

The founders' note, signed, with each name attached to the thing it is answerable for rather than to a title. A team section built from job titles tells the reader nothing they can act on; a short list of who answers for what tells them exactly who to write to when something breaks.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/team-founders-note`

Props:

- `note / contactLine`: string[] · string — The letter and how to reach them without a form.

Notes:
- Write accountability, not scope: "every plan it refuses to explain" beats "product and engineering".
- Deliberately still — a founders' note that animates is a founders' note nobody believes.
- Two or three founders. Past that it is a leadership grid, which is a different section.

### Where We Are Team (KB-305) — `team-where-we-are`
Cities are trivia; coverage is information.

Where the team actually is, and — the useful part — which hours of the day that adds up to. A page of city names is trivia; a page that says the team covers 06:00 to midnight UTC and names the six hours nobody is awake for tells a buyer in another timezone whether they will be answered.

Notes:

- Hours are pre-formatted strings in one stated zone, so the section never reads a clock.
- The total is derived from the places; it cannot disagree with the rows.

### Principles List Content (KB-306) — `content-principles-list`
A principle without a cost is a value.

Operating principles with the price of each one attached. Any company can publish four admirable sentences; a principle only becomes information when it says what it costs the people who wrote it — the office view that stays plain, the mornings that arrive flagged, the customers who leave easily.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/content-principles-list`

Props:
- `principles`: Principle[] — Each rule with the thing it costs to keep.
- `costLabel`: string — Caption over the cost line.

Notes:
- Without `costsUs` this is a values page, and nobody has ever believed one.
- Name a real cost — a competitor's advantage, a lost account, a capped growth rate.
- Four rules. Ten is a manifesto, and a manifesto settles no arguments.

### Glossary Content (KB-307) — `content-glossary`
Map their vocabulary onto yours.

The words this product uses and what they actually mean — with the term people use elsewhere printed beside each one, so a reader can map their own vocabulary onto yours rather than guessing. Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/content-glossary`

Notes:

- Define words whose familiar meaning would mislead. Defining obvious ones reads as padding.
- Say why a word was chosen when the choice carries meaning; that is the definition doing real work.

### Connect Time Integrations (KB-308) — `integrations-connect-time`

### Grouped Rollup Table (KB-310) — `datatable-grouped-rollup`

### Inline Edit Table (KB-311) — `datatable-inline-edit`

### Sign In Page (KP-001) — `auth-sign-in`

- `sentHeadline / sentCopy`: string — The confirmed state — deliberately never "we found your account".

Notes:
- Keep the identical response on the server too. A page careful in the UI and chatty in the API has leaked anyway.
- Explaining the vagueness is the point — an unexplained non-answer reads as a bug and gets retried.
- Never confirm or deny the address exists, including through timing or status codes.

### Second Factor Page (KP-004) — `auth-second-factor`
Recovery is not a footnote.

The second factor, with the lost-device path given the same weight as the code field. Almost every 2FA screen buries recovery in small grey text at the bottom, which is precisely where nobody looks while holding a dead phone.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/auth-second-factor`

Props:
- `length`: number — Digits in the code; drives the pattern and the shape check.
- `recoveryLabel / recoveryCopy / recoveryHref`: string — The lost-device path, at equal weight.

Notes:
- The shape check is digits and length only. It is not verification and must never be treated as any.
- autoComplete="one-time-code" lets phones offer the code — dropping it costs real completions.
- Give recovery its own heading and box. Grey small print at the bottom of a 2FA page is unreachable by design.

### Workspace Picker Page (KP-005) — `auth-workspace-pick`
Your role, before you click.

The workspace picker, which exists because "you are in more than one organisation" is a normal state most products treat as an edge case. Each row carries the role you hold there, and the account you are signed in as is stated at the top — because the commonest cause of an empty list is the wrong account.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/auth-workspace-pick`

Props:
- `workspaces`: Workspace[] — Name, your role there, yard count, and whether it is live.
- `signedInAs / missingLine`: string — Which account this is, and the path when the expected workspace is absent.

Notes:
- Print the role. Which workspace lets you do the thing you signed in for is the entire question this page answers.
- State the signed-in address prominently — the wrong account is the commonest cause of a missing workspace.
- Do not auto-forward on a single workspace without saying so; a page that vanishes is a page people cannot get back to.

### First Run Onboarding Page (KP-006) — `onboarding-first-run`
Always leave the door open.

The first session, asked one question at a time, with a way out at the top. The escape hatch is the part that matters: onboarding that cannot be skipped is a wall, and the people most likely to hit it are the ones setting up their second yard who already know all the answers.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/onboarding-first-run`

Props:
- `showPreview`: boolean — Render the live-bound preview card beside the questions.
- `skipLabel / skipHref`: string — The escape hatch, kept at the top rather than the bottom.
- `onDone`: (answers) => void — Fired with everything gathered.

Notes:
- Never remove the skip. Onboarding that cannot be skipped is a wall, and repeat users hit it hardest.
- The questions belong to stepform-one-question — pass it your own set rather than restyling this page.

### Import or Start Onboarding Page (KP-007) — `onboarding-import-or-start`
Three ways in, none of them a door that locks.

The fork at the start: bring something over, start clean, or look around first — each with its cost in minutes and what it needs from you. Products that force the import path lose everyone without their data to hand, and products that hide it lose everyone who has it.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/onboarding-import-or-start`

Props:
- `routes`: StartRoute[] — Each path with its effort, prerequisites, and whether it is suggested.
- `reversibleLine`: string — The line that makes the choice safe to make quickly.

Notes:
- Always offer a look-around route. Some people will not type anything until they have seen the thing work.
- State the minutes. A path without a cost is a path people avoid in case it is the long one.
- Suggest exactly one route — two suggestions is no suggestion.

### Invite Crew Onboarding Page (KP-008) — `onboarding-invite-crew`
State what a role cannot do.

Inviting the team, with each role's powers stated in full before anyone is added: what it can do, and — the half almost every invite screen omits — what it cannot. Permissions are the thing people get wrong at setup and discover months later.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/onboarding-invite-crew`

Props:
- `roles`: InviteRole[] — Each role with both its powers and its limits.
- `onSend / whatTheyGetLine`: (invites) => void · string — The send hook, and what the invitee actually receives.

Notes:
- The `cannot` half is not optional — it is the only reason this screen beats a dropdown of role names.
- Duplicate addresses are refused with a reason rather than silently merged.
- Say what an invite creates and when it expires; an invite with unstated terms gets forwarded around.

### About Story Page (KP-009) — `about-story`
Failures on the same page as the origin story.

The about page as an argument rather than a brochure: why the product exists, who answers for it, the numbers behind the claim, and — unusually for an about page — the incidents. A company willing to put its failures on the same page as its origin story is making a claim its competitors mostly cannot copy.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/about-story`

Props:
- `className`: string — The page composes shipped sections; pass content through each section's own props.

Notes:
- Every section here is a shipped block. If this page needs markup a section could own, that is a missing section rather than page-local styling.
- The incident log is the unusual choice and the reason the page works — moving it to a separate status page loses the effect.
- Order matters: why, who, how much, what went wrong, what now.

### How We Work Page (KP-010) — `about-how-we-work`
The operating manual, published.

The operating manual, published: the rules and what they cost, the words used carefully, where the team is and which hours that leaves uncovered, who does what during a rollout, and where the data sits. The page a careful buyer reads second — after they believe the product works and before they believe the company will still be here.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/about-how-we-work`

Props:
- `className`: string — Composes shipped sections; pass content through each section's props.

Notes:
- Pair it with about-story rather than merging them — one argues why, this one argues how.
- Keep data residency last. It is the section people arrive looking for and the one they leave satisfied by.

### Careers Index Page (KP-011) — `careers-index`
Help the wrong people leave.

Careers written to help the wrong people leave: the bench and its empty seats, where the team is and the hours nobody covers, the rules and what they cost, and a fit section naming who this is not for. A careers page optimised for volume produces a funnel full of people who resign in a year.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/careers-index`

Props:
- `className`: string — Composes shipped sections; pass content through each section's props.

Notes:
- The fit and objection sections ship with marketing copy — replace their content with hiring equivalents. The shapes are the point, and both take typed props.
- Publishing the uncovered hours is a feature here: candidates in those timezones deserve to know before applying.

### Careers Role Page (KP-012) — `careers-role`
Ninety seconds to rule yourself out.

A single role, written so the wrong applicant can rule themselves out in ninety seconds: the pay stated, the interview loop described, what the person will actually do in their first months, and a list of what is not being asked for. That last list is why this page gets fewer, better applications.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/careers-role`

Props:
- `facts / doing / notAsking`: RoleFact[] · string[] — The particulars, the first ninety days, and what is not required.
- `payLine`: string — The band, stated. A role page without one wastes both sides' time.

Notes:
- Publish the band. Every conversation that starts without it is a conversation about the wrong thing.
- The not-asking list is the differentiator — it is what makes the rest of the page believable.
- The interview loop uses how-plain-steps, so the hiring process is described in the same shape as the product's.

### Changelog Timeline Page (KP-013) — `changelog-timeline`
Ask for the fixes alone.

The changelog as a running record, filterable by what kind of change you came looking for. Most changelogs bury fixes under features; this one lets a reader ask for fixes alone, which is what someone chasing a bug they reported actually wants — and it means the fixes have to be written well enough to stand on their own.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/changelog-timeline`

Props:
- `releases`: Release[] — Each release with its tagged lines.

Notes:
- Releases with nothing matching the filter drop out entirely, so the page never shows an empty release card.
- Write fixes to stand alone — under a fixes-only filter there is no feature copy to carry them.
- Dates are pre-formatted strings; the page never touches a clock.

### Single Release Page (KP-014) — `changelog-release`
The migration note goes first.

One release at length, with breaking changes given their own block at the top rather than a footnote at the bottom, and the fixes listed in full. Release notes that lead with features and bury the migration note are how integrations break quietly on a Tuesday.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/changelog-release`

Props:
- `breaking`: BreakingChange[] — What changed and what the reader must do — rendered at the top.
- `notes / fixes`: ReleaseNote[] · string[] — The long-form notes and the plain fix list.

Notes:
- Breaking changes render before the narrative. A migration note at the foot of a release is one nobody read.
- Every breaking entry needs an action and a date, or it is an announcement rather than a warning.
- List the fixes even when they are embarrassing; that is what makes the feature notes believable.

### Version Compare Page (KP-015) — `changelog-compare`
See the size of the upgrade first.

What changed between two versions, laid flat: the subject, what it was, what it is, and whether you have to do anything. Anyone upgrading across several releases has to read every note in between and hold the diff in their head; this page holds it for them, and counts the breaking rows so the size of the job is visible before they start.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/changelog-compare`

Props:
- `rows`: VersionRow[] — Subject, before, after, and whether it needs action.
- `versions / defaultFrom / defaultTo`: string[] · string — The selectable versions and the opening pair.

Notes:
- Picking a target at or behind the source is answered explicitly rather than silently showing an identical diff.
- The breaking count is derived from the rows — it cannot disagree with the table.
- Never remove a shape without a release that carries both; say so on the page.

### Blog Index Page (KP-016) — `blog-index`
Lead on the post-mortem.

The writing index, led by the post the company would rather not lead with. A blog that opens on a launch announcement tells the reader it exists to market; one that opens on a post-mortem tells them it exists to be read, and the second is the only reason anyone subscribes.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/blog-index`

Props:
- `posts`: Post[] — Mark exactly one as `lead`; it is set larger at the top.

Notes:
- Lead on something that cost you something. An index that opens on a launch reads as a press page.
- The signup at the foot is newsletter-back-issues, so the archive is proof rather than a promise.
- Read times are part of the offer; publish them honestly.

### Blog Post Page (KP-017) — `blog-post`
Corrections where the error was read.

A long-form post with the correction notice at the top rather than appended as a footnote nobody scrolls to. Everything else is deliberately plain — the reading measure, the pull quote on the balance instrument, and nothing that moves while someone is trying to read.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/blog-post`

Props:
- `blocks`: PostBlock[] — Paragraphs, headings, lists, and quotes in reading order.
- `correction`: string — Rendered at the top, not the foot.

Notes:
- A correction at the foot is only seen by people who already finished — which is not who it is for.
- Pull quotes belong to balance-quote; never re-set one as styled text.
- Nothing animates during reading on purpose. The cascade belongs on index pages, not inside prose.

### Blog Archive Page (KP-018) — `blog-archive`
A finding tool, not a showcase.

The whole archive, filterable by topic and grouped by year — the page for someone who has decided this is worth reading properly and wants the post they half-remember. Deliberately dense and deliberately still: an archive is a finding tool, and every animation between a reader and a list of titles is a tax on that.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/blog-archive`

Props:
- `entries`: ArchiveEntry[] — Every post with its year and topic.

Notes:
- Topics and years are both derived from the entries, so filtering never strands an empty year heading.
- Rows only reflow on layout — an archive that animates its list fights the person scanning it.
- Keep everything. An archive with posts quietly removed is not an archive.

### Not Found Page (KP-019) — `error-not-found`
Three destinations beat one front door.

The 404, built on the library's own radar sweep, with somewhere to go underneath it. A 404 offering only a way home sends people to the top of a site they were already deep inside — the three most likely destinations are worth more than the front door.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/error-not-found`

Props:
- `face`: "radar" | "shatter" | "elastic" | "echo" | "bands" | "spotlight" — Threaded to the not-found block; radar is the default.

Notes:
- The sweep belongs to the not-found block; this page contributes the destinations under it.
- Name real destinations. Generic links are the same dead end with more words.

### Server Fault Page (KP-020) — `error-server-fault`
Give them something to quote.

The 500, written as a report rather than an apology: a reference code the reader can quote, a plain statement that we already know, and a link to the status page. A page that only says something went wrong tells the reader nothing they did not know and leaves them nothing to say when they write in.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/error-server-fault`

Notes:
- The reference is the point — without one, support conversations start with which page and roughly when.
- Say you already know. Most people write in only because they assume nobody noticed.
- Never claim data was lost or saved unless it is true; say only what you actually know.

### Maintenance Page (KP-021) — `error-maintenance`
Planned, so it can promise an end.

The maintenance page, which differs from an outage page in the one way that matters: this was planned, so it can say when it ends and what still works. No countdown — a ticking clock turns a scheduled ninety minutes into an emergency in the reader's head.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/error-maintenance`

Notes:
- Deliberately no countdown. A clock ticking down reads as an emergency rather than a schedule.
- The still-working list is what decides whether anyone has to change their day.
- The window is a pre-formatted string in one stated zone; the page never reads a clock.

### Offline Page (KP-022) — `error-offline`
Lead with what they still have.

Offline, told from the yard's point of view: a shed with no signal is a normal Tuesday, not an error. So this page leads with what is still readable from the cache and what is being held to send later, rather than with an apology for physics.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/error-offline`

Notes:
- Lead with the cache, not the apology. Losing signal is normal where this product lives.
- Show the queue. People will not trust an offline write they cannot see.
- Cache timestamps are pre-formatted; the page never reads a clock.

### Rate Limited Page (KP-023) — `error-rate-limited`
Stop them seeing it twice.

The 429, written as a diagnosis: which limit was hit, how far over, when it resets, and — the part that actually helps — the three things that stop it happening again. A rate limit page that only says too many requests is a page the same caller will see again in sixty seconds.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/error-rate-limited`

Notes:
- The remedies are the page. Without them the same caller returns in a minute.
- State the exact limit and its scope — per token, per minute, which API.
- Say plainly that nothing is penalised; most people read a 429 as a ban.

### Expired Link Page (KP-024) — `error-link-expired`
The link did its job.

An expired one-time link, which is a success rather than a failure and should read like one: the link did exactly what it was built to do. The page says which kind of link it was, why it expires, and offers a new one in a single press.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/error-link-expired`

Notes:
- Offer the replacement in one press. The reader is holding a dead link and wants another, not an explanation of tokens.
- Explain the expiry — it turns a frustration into a reassurance about their account.
- Name which kind of link it was, or the reader cannot tell what to ask for again.

### Deleted Resource Page (KP-025) — `error-resource-deleted`
Not lost — removed, by someone, at a time.

Gone, but accounted for: what it was, who removed it, when, and whether it can still come back. A deleted resource that 404s silently makes people think the system lost it — naming the person and the moment turns a suspected bug into a decision someone made.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/error-resource-deleted`

Notes:
- Name who and when. Anonymous deletion reads as data loss and generates a support ticket.
- State the restore window explicitly, including what survives after it closes.
- Only offer restore when it will actually work; a dead button here is worse than none.

### Unsupported Browser Page (KP-026) — `error-browser-unsupported`
Name the capability, not the browser.

The unsupported-browser page, which names the missing capability rather than the browser. Gate screens that sniff user agents are wrong within a year and insult anyone on a browser they did not choose — a yard PC is usually locked by an IT policy the reader cannot change.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/error-browser-unsupported`

Notes:
- Name the missing capability. User-agent sniffing is wrong within a year and blames the reader for an IT policy.
- Always offer a fallback that works anywhere — a printable view, a plain list, something.
- Version floors go beside each browser, or the list is not actionable.

### Region Blocked Page (KP-027) — `error-region-blocked`
Show the detection, and how to correct it.

Region-blocked, with the two things such pages almost always omit: what region the request appeared to come from, and what to do when that is wrong. Geolocation is routinely mistaken — a VPN, a satellite link, a ship — and a page with no correction path strands the people most likely to be misidentified.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/error-region-blocked`

Notes:
- Show what was detected. Without it a false positive is unarguable.
- The correction path is the important half — geolocation is wrong often enough to strand real customers.
- State the reason as policy or law; unavailable in your region alone reads as arbitrary.

### Atlas Sign-Up Page (KP-028) — `auth-atlas`
Other people are already here.

Account creation beside a live activity map: the form says what the account creates before it creates it, and the atlas beside it — the library's point globe with a few pips and a count of crews online — says the quieter thing, that other people are already here. Validation is inline and plain, the strength line describes rather than scores, and a passkey path is offered as text instead of a wall of provider buttons.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/auth-atlas`

Props:
- `pips / crews`: AtlasPip[] · number — The yards shown on the atlas and the online count it steps toward.
- `onSubmit`: (values) => void — Receives the name and email; the page never handles a password itself.

Notes:
- A shell — wire onSubmit to your own auth and never handle credentials client-side.
- The globe is point-globe doing reassurance duty; it is decorative and hidden from assistive tech.
- Reduced motion keeps the globe's own fallback; the count still steps.

### Instrument Template (KT-001) — `template-instrument`
Eleven sections, one argument.

The full argument, top to bottom, for a product that has to be believed before it is bought: claim, proof of who runs it, what it does, how a day goes, the same morning before and after, the numbers, one customer at length, price, the four honest questions, and two doors out.

### Launch Template (KT-002) — `template-launch`

One announcement, one ask, and as little else as the page can survive on. Deliberately short — for the weeks when there is not much to show, a long page mostly advertises how little there is, and the only conversion that matters is the address.

### Agent Template (KT-003) — `template-agent`
Demonstrated in its own medium.

For products whose core act is a conversation: the hero is a live composer, how-it-works is a transcript the reader advances, and pricing is metered in work rather than seats. The incident log sits mid-page on purpose — anything acting on a customer's behalf has to answer for acting wrongly.

### Studio Template (KT-004) — `template-studio`

### Ledger Template (KT-005) — `template-ledger`
The table on the page actually sorts.

For instruments rather than apps: the product is shown working — a real sortable grid, a trend per row, standings that re-rank — before it is described. Buyers of data tools have been shown too many screenshots, and the fastest way past that is a page where the table on it actually sorts.

### Field Template (KT-006) — `template-field`
Everything given away, and the close still lands.

The honest play, assembled: the price in the first screen, where that money goes in the second, who the product is not for in the third, and the failures published before anyone asks. Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/template-field`

### Agent Skill — `agent-skill`
The library, taught to your agent.

A packaged skill that teaches a coding agent the whole system in one install: discovering the catalog through MCP or the machine metadata, picking components by the verb their spring performs, installing by serial or slug, and composing under the five-spring doctrine. Installs to .claude/skills/kinetiq/SKILL.md; pairs with the agents-rules item, which carries the full operating rules.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/agent-skill`

### Figure runtime — `figure`
Three, loaded only when a figure asks for it.

The lazy 3D runtime behind the figures: loads three and its loaders after mount, builds preset shapes or sniffs a GLB, glTF, SVG, or image by its bytes, and stages the object under studio light with orbit and idle motion.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/figure`

### Paint — `paint`
The interface, painted so a shader can hold it.

The DOM painter behind the effects wing: rasterises a live subtree — backgrounds, borders, text laid out by the browser itself, images, inline SVG — onto a canvas so a shader can sample the interface as a texture. Every browser, no experimental flag; what it will and will not paint is a stated contract.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/paint`

### GLSL Helper — `glsl`
A shader is the whole effect; this is the rest.

The WebGL2 vocabulary every effect composes: programs with useful error output, uniform setting by arity, a fullscreen pass with DOM-oriented texture coordinates, indexed grid meshes for cloth and tiles, framebuffers that fall back from half-float to bytes and say so, resize, context loss, and disposal that deletes exactly what it made.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/glsl`

### usePaintedSurface — `use-painted-surface`
A texture you can trust the version of.

Owns a painter for a ref and mirrors its version into React, so an effect uploads a texture only after a completed paint and never samples a half-drawn one.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/use-painted-surface`

### Tactile Sound — `tactile-sound`
Sounds made on the spot, only when asked.

Interface sounds synthesised on the spot with Web Audio: ticks, clacks, pops, whooshes, chimes and continuous voices, built from oscillators, noise and filters when they play. Silent by default, no audio context until a sound is asked for inside a gesture, quiet when the page is hidden, throttled per voice, and compressed on the master bus.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/tactile-sound`

### Tactile Gesture — `tactile-gesture`
One drag, one throw, one edge.

The hand-feel the Tactile components share: a drag that follows the pointer 1:1 and captures it only after a few pixels, release velocity measured over the last moments of the drag, throw projection, and rubber-band resistance past an edge.

Install: `pnpm dlx shadcn@latest add @kinetiq/tactile-gesture`
